title: Reducing yield ratio while enhancing strength in 500MPa grade wind power steel via intercritical annealing
abstract: This study achieved a favourable combination of high strength and a low yield ratio on a novel wind power steel subjected to a single-step intercritical annealing (IA) followed by water cooling strategy. The microstructure, mechanical properties and strain-hardening behavior of the steel were investigated before and after IA. Results showed that the experimental steel was transformed from a bainitic structure to a ferrite-martensite dual-phase (DP) steel. As the annealing temperature increased to 800 °C, the tensile strength increased significantly from 732MPa to 877MPa, while the yield ratio decreased effectively from 0.85 to 0.52. The former is attributed to the high volume fraction of martensite, while the latter is primarily due to the chain-like networked martensite distribution which enhances ductility and strain-hardening capacity. Finally, strain-hardening characteristics were analyzed using the Hollomon and modified Crussard-Jaoul (MC-J) models. The results indicate that the MC-J model demonstrated a superior fit for the ferrite-martensite DP steel. In conclusion, single-step IA is proven to be an effective heat treatment for optimizing the mechanical properties of wind power steels.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Wind power steel refers to a class of high-strength low-alloy (HSLA) steel that is widely used for wind energy infrastructure due to its superior balance of strength, ductility, and weldability  [1–3] . Driven by the global pursuit of higher power generation efficiency, wind turbine towers are evolving toward larger scales and greater heights, imposing more stringent requirements on the mechanical properties of wind power steels  [4,5] . To meet these escalating demands, a novel 500 MPa grade wind power steel with a bainitic microstructure was recently developed via thermo-mechanically controlled processing (TMCP), offering significantly higher strength than conventional ferrite-pearlite steels  [6,7] . However, this strength enhancement is often accompanied by an increase in the yield ratio (YR)  [6] . For instance, in a Nb-Ti microalloyed steel, the yield strength increased from 476 to 537 MPa while the YR also increased from 0.70 to 0.78  [8] . Due to safety concerns, wind power steels require a low YR to provide high resistance against sudden strength loss caused by plastic instability  [9,10] . Accordingly, it is imperative to explore effective methods to balance the YR and strength in wind power steels for industrial applications.

Tailoring heterogeneous microstructures in steels (e.g., dual-phase alloys) is an effective strategy to optimize the YR  [11] . The most direct approach is to modulate the volume fraction of the constituent phases. For example, introducing a soft phase into a hard matrix effectively lowers the YR but inevitably entails a loss in strength. As reported by Li et al.  [12] , increasing the ferrite fraction lowered the YR to 0.66 but significantly compromised both yield and tensile strength. Similarly, Xie et al.  [13]  achieved an ultra-low yield ratio of 0.54 by introducing 13% retained austenite into a low-carbon steel, but at the expense of a yield strength reduction of nearly 450 MPa. To overcome this trade-off, researchers have turned their attention to optimizing the morphology and distribution of the constituent phases. Specifically, Park et al.  [14]  found that transitioning the martensite distribution from isolated islands to a continuous networked structure leads to a simultaneous improvement in strength and a reduction in YR, with almost no change to the overall phase fraction. This networked structure facilitates a more homogeneous strain partitioning between the ferrite and hard martensite phases, thereby augmenting both the strength and ductility  [15,16] . Furthermore, grain refinement offers a synergistic route to simultaneously increase strength and decrease the YR. Son et al.  [17]  applied a quenching-IA sequence to a low-carbon steel pre-treated by equal channel angular pressing (ECAP), attaining a remarkable YR of 0.52 alongside a 200 MPa increase in tensile strength.

Generally, these heterogeneous microstructures can be achieved through intercritical heat treatment (IHT), which has emerged as a practical strategy for HSLA steels  [18,19] . Various protocols have demonstrated remarkable efficacy in suppressing the YR. Yu et al.  [20]  integrated IA between quenching (Q) and tempering (T), successfully reducing the YR from 0.93 to 0.85; Zhu et al.  [21] , Tang et al.  [22] , and Wang et al.  [23]  employed IA before tempering to lower the YR while maintaining high strength in TMCP-produced HSLA steels; moreover, Ohaeri et al.  [24]  and Yadav et al.  [25]  demonstrated that a two-step IA can effectively reduce the YR below 0.7. However, considering the massive scale of wind power infrastructure, the industrial implementation of such sophisticated multi-step schemes is severely restricted by high energy consumption, operational costs, and stringent environmental policies. For the wind power steel plates produced via TMCP, it is imperative to develop a more streamlined and cost-effective process. Previous studies have found that short-time austenitization followed by quenching  [26]  or single-step IA  [16]  can refine microstructures and significantly lower the YR and enhance the strength in low-carbon steels. Nevertheless, such investigations primarily focused on the cold-rolled steels with ferrite-pearlite microstructures, with less attention paid to TMCP-produced bainitic steels. Furthermore, prior research has revealed that the preferential growth of reverted austenite occurs along the bainitic lath boundaries. This microstructural inheritance may facilitate the formation of the desired networked structure in bainitic steels  [27] . Therefore, the single-step IA is a viable strategy for this newly developed wind power steel.

Aiming to optimize both strength and YR, the present study investigates the application of a single-step IA to modify the as-manufactured microstructure of a novel 500 MPa grade wind power steel. Multiple characterization techniques were employed to examine the effect of different holding temperatures on the resultant microstructure evolution and consequently on the relevant mechanical properties. This research provides strategic insights into the selection of heat treatment protocols for steels manufactured via TMCP.

sections.heading: Experimental materials
paragraphs:
The chemical composition of the 500 MPa grade wind power steel plate investigated in the study is listed in  
                         Table 1 . The steel plate, with a thickness of 25 mm, was manufactured via TMCP. Prior to heat treatment, cylindrical specimens with dimensions of Φ15 mm × 92 mm were machined from the as-received steel plates.

sections.heading: Heat treatments
paragraphs:
The calculated phase fraction versus temperature diagram for the experimental steel, determined using Thermo-Calc software (TCFE7 database), is shown in  
                         Fig. 1 (a). The Ac 1  temperature (starting temperature of the BCC-FCC phase transformation) and the Ac 3  temperature (finishing temperature) of the experimental steel are 695 °C and 821 °C, respectively. A schematic representation of the single-step IA process is presented in  Fig. 1 (b). Specimens were heated to 720, 750, and 800 °C, held for 15 min at each temperature, and subsequently water-cooled. In this study, the as-received specimens were labeled as AR, while those subjected to IA at different temperatures were designated as IA-720, IA-750, and IA-800.

sections.heading: Mechanical tests
paragraphs:
Tensile specimens were prepared from the as-received steel plates in accordance with Chinese Standard (GB/T 228.1-2021). The geometry of the uniaxially tensile specimens is shown in  
                         Fig. 2 . The surfaces of all specimens were ground with emery papers to minimize the influence of residual stress on the mechanical behavior. Tensile tests were conducted on an Instron 5982 static testing machine at a strain rate of 10 −3  s −1  at room temperature. At least 3 specimens per group were tested to guarantee the data reproducibility. Vickers microhardness was measured using a micro-hardness tester (AMH-43) under a load of 300 gram-force for 15 s. The average HV value was calculated from measurements at twenty different locations.

sections.heading: Microstructure characterization
paragraphs: Specimens for microstructural characterization were extracted from the deformation-free ends of the tensile specimens using wire-cut electrical discharge machining. Phase identification and dislocation density were evaluated by X-ray diffraction (XRD, SmartLab) using Cu  K α radiation at an operating voltage of 35 kV. The XRD patterns were recorded over a scanning range of 30°–110° at a speed of 4°/min. Microstructural features were further examined by a field-emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, Zeiss Sigma-500) equipped with electron backscattered diffraction (EBSD) detectors (SYMMETRY-S2) and a transmission electron microscope (TEM, JEM-2100Plus).

For XRD, SEM, and EBSD observations, samples were initially ground by emery papers (400#-2000#), and then polished with 2.5 μm diamond paste. Samples intended for SEM imaging were etched in a 4% nital solution for 10–12 s. Additionally, those designated for EBSD and XRD analyses were electropolished in a 10% perchloric acid-ethanol solution at 22 V for 17 s to remove the surface deformation layer. The SEM was operated at an accelerating voltage of 20 kV, with a step size of 0.2 μm utilized for EBSD mapping. TEM foils were mechanically thinned to approximately 50 μm and subsequently subjected to twin-jet polished in a 10% perchloric acid-ethanol solution at 25 V and −20 °C.

EBSD data post-processing was performed using AztecCrystal (v2.1) software. A critical misorientation threshold of 15° was defined for grain identification, with a minimum of 500 grains analyzed per map to ensure statistical significance. The volume fraction and average size of the constituent phases were quantified from SEM images using Image-Pro Plus (v6.0) software based on the line intercept method.

sections.heading: Microstructure characteristics
paragraphs:
Typical microstructures of AR, IA-720, IA-750 and IA-800 are displayed in  
                         Fig. 3 . The microstructure of AR primarily consists of bainite (B) with a small fraction of martensite-austenite (M-A) constituents and carbides dispersed within grains or along grain boundaries ( Fig. 3 (a1) and (a2)). In contrast, in the samples subjected to IA treatment, the bainite matrix was replaced by ferrite (F) and varying volume fractions of martensite (M), accompanied by the precipitation of carbides ( Fig. 3 (b1)–(d2)). Consequently, the experimental steel underwent a microstructural transition from a bainitic structure to a ferrite-martensite dual-phase configuration through IA. Notably, the martensite islands in IA-750 and IA-800 exhibit distinct distribution patterns. The martensite islands in IA-750 are predominantly located along grain boundaries ( Fig. 3 (c1) and (c2)), whereas in IA-800, they are not only distributed along the grain boundaries but also uniformly dispersed within the coarse ferrite ( Fig. 3 (d1) and (d2)). Moreover, the martensite islands in IA-800 encircle the ferrite grains, forming a continuous networked structure. A similar observation was also reported in a cold-rolled low-carbon steel subjected to IA  [16] . In comparison, the martensite islands in IA-750 exhibit a more isolated and discrete morphology. This divergence in martensite distribution is primarily due to the IA temperature. A higher temperature facilitates the growth of intragranular reverted austenite and its coalescence with intergranular reverted austenite  [27] . Thus, the interconnected austenite readily partitions the undissolved ferrite, encapsulating it to finally form the networked structure.

Fig. 4  presents the TEM observations of AR, IA-720, IA-750 and IA-800. Precipitates exhibit a spherical shape, with sizes varying from a few nanometers to nearly 50 nm, and tends to decrease in size as the IA temperature rises. Furthermore, statistical analysis derived from the TEM images indicates that the volume fraction of precipitates in IA-800 is higher than that in the other three samples, which is consistent with previous studies on intercritical heat treatment  [28,29] . In addition, coarse elliptical carbides were also observed in the matrices of both AR and IA-720 ( Fig. 4 (a) and (b)). The carbides in the AR sample measured only about 100 nm, whereas those in IA-720 coarsened to several hundred nanometers. This phenomenon is likely attributable to the relatively low annealing temperature, which provided insufficient driving force for complete dissolution, thereby promoting Ostwald ripening and carbon segregation. These TEM observations are consistent with the aforementioned SEM findings ( Fig. 3 ).

Fig. 5  displays the inverse pole figure (IPF) maps along the  Z -axis ( Fig. 5 (a1)–(d1)), the grain boundary (GB) misorientation distribution maps ( Fig. 5 (a2)–(d2)) and the Kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps ( Fig. 5 (a3)–(d3)). The IPF maps reveal that the grains in the AR sample exhibit a preferred orientation toward the <111> direction. As the annealing temperature increases, this texture intensity gradually weakens but is not entirely eliminated. Concurrently, the grain morphology undergoes a transition from the pancake-like structure observed in the AR sample toward a more equiaxed morphology ( Fig. 5 (a1)). However, in IA-800 the population of equiaxed grains decreases and the grains adopt a more needle-like morphology, as shown in  Fig. 5 (d1). In the grain boundary distribution maps ( Fig. 5 (a2)–(d2)), boundaries are categorized into three types based on the misorientation tolerance angle (MTA): red (2° < MTA < 15°), blue (15° < MTA < 45°) and black (MTA > 45°) lines. Specifically, boundaries with MTA between 2° and 15° are defined as low-angle grain boundaries (LAGBs), while those exceeding 15° are classified as high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs). It is evident that AR exhibits a high density of LAGBs in  Fig. 5 (a2), reflecting the high-density substructure developed during the controlled rolling process. In contrast, the IA-treated samples contain regions of equiaxed grains with minimal internal LAGBs, alongside grains that retain a relatively high density of substructures, indicating that partial recrystallization occurred during the IA process. KAM mapping quantifies the average angular misorientation between each pixel's crystallographic orientation and its eight adjacent neighboring pixels, providing a proxy for the geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs) density and local strain levels  [30] . The color gradient in the KAM maps ( Fig. 5 (a3)–(d3)), ranging from blue to bright green and red, corresponds to the transition from low to high levels of local strain. Notably, IA-750 and IA-800 exhibit a larger proportion of low-strain (blue) regions ( Fig. 5 (c3) and (d3)). Moreover, the high-strain zones in IA-800 are distributed more uniformly compared with the localized strain distribution in IA-750.

Fig. 6 (a) shows the volume fraction of the constituent phases in the samples AR, IA-720, IA-750 and IA-800. Accounting for the existence of carbides, the total volume fraction of the primary constituent phases is slightly less than 100%. The volume fraction of martensite ( V 
                         M ) increases with the IA temperature, measuring 2.3%, 5.9%, 18.2%, and 41.6% for samples AR through IA-800, respectively.  Fig. 6 (b) presents the average grain size of the bainite/ferrite and martensite islands. With increasing IA temperature, the average grain size of ferrite exhibits an initial increase followed by a subsequent decrease. The maximum average ferrite grain size is observed in IA-750 (4.77 μm), while the minimum is found in IA-800 (2.96 μm). Specifically, the corresponding average bainite/ferrite grain sizes of AR, IA-720, IA-750 and IA-800 are 3.96, 4.65, 4.77, and 2.96 μm, respectively. Concurrently, the average size of the martensite islands shows a consistent upward trend, measuring 0.86, 1.09, 1.65, and 2.24 μm, respectively, showing an increasing trend. The number fraction of different types of GBs is given in  Fig. 6 (c). The results reveal a declining proportion of LAGBs and a corresponding increase in the proportion of HAGBs. The highest number fraction of LAGBs, observed in the AR sample, is attributed to the deformation substructures generated during the TMCP controlled rolling process, while the significant decline in the LAGB fraction of IA-750 indicates relatively pronounced recrystallization during the isothermal holding stage. In IA-800, the substantial increase in the fraction of GBs with MTA > 45° is in good agreement with the elevated martensite content. Finally,  Fig. 6 (d) presents the average KAM values of the different samples. The average KAM value decreases from 0.73 in the AR sample to 0.51 in IA-750 but rebounds to 0.53 in IA-800.

                         Fig. 7 (a). No distinct diffraction peaks associated with the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure were detected in any of the samples. This is primarily attributed to the low carbon content and limited alloying additions in the experimental steel, which compromise the thermodynamic stability of the austenite phase during the cooling stage, leading to its transformation into other phases. As shown in  Fig. 7 (b), the dislocation densities of AR, IA-720, IA-750 and IA-800 were calculated to be 4.66 × 10 14 , 1.95 × 10 14 , 1.06 × 10 14 , and 2.74 × 10 14  m −2 , respectively. Following intercritical annealing, the dislocation density initially decreases, which is primarily attributed to recovery and recrystallization during the isothermal holding stage. However, the volume expansion associated with the austenite-to-martensite transformation induces plastic deformation in the adjacent ferrite matrix. This process introduces additional GNDs, thereby leading to an increase in the overall dislocation density in IA-800. Notably, the dislocation density and average KAM values exhibit a consistent trend, further corroborating this microstructural evolution.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The tensile properties and microhardness of AR, IA-720, IA-750 and IA-800 are plotted in  
                         Fig. 8  with the corresponding data listed in  
                         Table 2 . As shown in  Fig. 8 (a), IA-720 exhibits a yield plateau, whereas AR, IA-750 and IA-800 display continuous yielding behavior. Interestingly, the yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS) exhibit divergent trends as a function of the IA temperature. Specifically, the YS decreases monotonically from 622 MPa (AR) to 459 MPa (IA-800). In contrast, the UTS initially decreases from 734 MPa (AR) to 638 MPa at 720 °C before rising progressively with increasing IA temperature. The maximum UTS of 877 MPa is achieved at 800 °C, representing an approximately 20% increase compared with the AR sample ( Fig. 8 (b)). Regarding ductility, the total elongation (TE) increases by 33% (from 21.3% to 28.3%) in IA-720, reaches a minimum (20.1%) in IA-750, and subsequently rebounds to 23.3% in IA-800. Notably, the uniform elongation (UE) of all three IA specimens was improved, exceeding that of AR by 50%, 37%, and 39%, respectively. The average Vickers hardness values exhibit a trend consistent with the UTS variations, decreasing from AR to IA-720 before increasing significantly in IA-750 and IA-800 ( Table 2 ).

sections.heading: Analysis of ultimate tensile strength
paragraphs: UTS is primarily governed by the composite strength of the constituent phases  [51] . In the case of IA-720, the IA treatment promoted the decomposition of bainite into ferrite and carbides. This ferrite exhibits lower strength compared with the original bainitic ferrite. Furthermore, the relatively coarse, elliptical or rod-like carbides potentially serve as preferential sites for crack nucleation. Despite the slight increase in martensite volume fraction, the strength increment provided by the secondary phases is insufficient to compensate for the softening effect of the matrix decomposition. Thus, the UTS of IA-720 deteriorated significantly compared with the AR sample, representing the lowest value among all samples. In contrast, for IA-750 and IA-800, the UTS is enhanced primarily due to the markedly higher volume fraction of the martensite phase. Moreover, grain refinement also contributes to the improvement in UTS, as a finer grain structure increases the density of grain boundaries. These boundaries, particularly high-angle grain boundaries (HAGBs), act as effective barriers to dislocation movement and retard crack propagation  [52] . As shown in  Fig. 6 (c), the number fraction of HAGBs increases with the IA temperature. Consequently, IA-750 and IA-800 exhibit significantly higher UTS compared with IA-720. Owing to the substantially higher martensite content in IA-800, it achieves the maximum UTS recorded in this study.

sections.heading: Analysis of the elongation discrepancy between IA-750 and IA-800
paragraphs: A simultaneous increase in UTS and elongation is observed in IA-800 compared with IA-750, which deviates from the conventional trade-off relationship between strength and ductility. This deviation is ascribed to the difference in martensite distribution. As displayed in  Fig. 3 (c1)–(d2), the martensite in IA-750 exhibits an isolated morphology, whereas in IA-800, it presents a networked structure. There is a distinct difference in terms of strain partitioning between isolated and networked martensite distributions  [14,15] . In regions with isolated martensite, slip deformation is prone to occur within the interconnected ferrite matrix. This ease of deformation within the ferrite facilitates local stress relaxation, resulting in relatively lower stress partitioned into the martensite. Consequently, heterogeneous deformation develops in these regions. In the case of the networked martensite distribution, the slip deformation of ferrite grains is effectively hindered by the harder martensite islands. This hindrance promotes stress partitioning into the martensite and triggers earlier plastic deformation of martensite islands, leading to more homogeneous deformation throughout the microstructure. Furthermore, the networked martensite structure provides a higher strain hardening capacity, which effectively hardens the necking region. By suppressing premature strain localization and facilitating the propagation of deformation to adjacent regions, the networked morphology delays the onset of fracture  [14] . Hence, IA-800 exhibits enhanced ductility. It is worth noting that, although the finest ferrite grain size was achieved in IA-800, the total elongation remains largely unaffected by grain refinement alone, in alignment with previous findings  [53] . The strain hardening behavior will be further investigated in  Section 3.4 .

sections.heading: Effect of IA on the YR
paragraphs:
In the present study, a desirable combination of a low YR and enhanced tensile strength was successfully achieved in IA-800. Specifically, IA-800 exhibits a YR of 0.52 and a tensile strength of 877 MPa, representing the optimal balance of mechanical properties among the four samples. As shown in

It can be seen that an excellent balance of a high tensile strength and a low YR was achieved in IA-800. Although several steels display a higher tensile strength than IA-800, their YR values (exceeding 0.75) are significantly higher than IA-800.

With increasing IA temperature, the formation of a higher volume fraction of martensite leads to a significant decrease in  b . Hence, the downward trend of  b  with temperature contributes to lowering the YR, particularly in IA-750 and IA-800. Additionally, some previous studies  [12,61]  suggest that the addition of the hard, low-temperature transformation phases (e.g., martensite) to a ductile ferrite matrix can diminish the parameter  N , thereby elevating the YR. The approximately 10% decrease in the  N  value observed in IA-720 compared with IA-750 is in agreement with these previous findings. However, the stability of  N  values in IA-750 and IA-800 implies the existence of competing factors that counteract the decline in  N , given that IA-800 contained a considerably larger amount of martensite than IA-750. This phenomenon can be ascribed to the aforementioned variation in martensite distribution. The high proportion of networked martensite in IA-800 promotes higher strain hardening capacity, thus enhancing the uniform elongation ( Table 2 )  [14] . As mentioned previously, the value of  N  is primarily determined by the uniform elongation. Hence, the networked martensite distribution is instrumental in suppressing the decline of  N , thereby promoting to lower the YR, in alignment with earlier observations  [62] .

To summarize, the lowest YR achieved in IA-800 stems from a two-fold mechanism: firstly, the reduction in  b  induced by the high martensite volume fraction; and secondly, the preservation of  N  facilitated by the networked martensite distribution.

sections.heading: Strain-hardening behavior
paragraphs: Strain hardening behavior is crucial to characterizing the deformation mechanisms of steels. To elucidate the strain hardening behavior of specimens subjected to different IA temperatures, the conventional Hollomon analysis and MC-J analytical method were employed herein  [63,64] . The data beyond yielding point were utilized for the analyses. For IA-720, the data following the yielding platform were analyzed.

It is observed that AR and IA-720 exhibit one-stage linear strain hardening behavior, while IA-750 and IA-800 follow a two-stage strain hardening regime, a phenomenon widely reported for DP steels  [65–67] . The strain hardening exponent  n  in Stage I exhibits an increasing trend from AR to IA-800. A similar correlation is also observed in Stage II when comparing IA-750 and IA-800.

Generally speaking, the strain hardening behavior of steels is affected by their characteristics of constituent phases, including their hardness, volume fraction and morphology  [68] . These phases can be classified as soft or hard based on their relative hardness. When subjected to external loading, the soft phase tends to deform earlier while the hard phase resists deformation, resulting in inhomogeneous deformation between phases and thus strain gradients  [69] . To maintain microstructural continuity, GNDs are introduced, which contribute to the strain hardening by impeding dislocation glide and creating long-range back-stress  [70] . Consequently, the existence of a hard second phase (e.g., martensite) can effectively enhance the strain hardening ability of steels with a ferritic matrix  [71] . Furthermore, some previous studies found that an increase in  V 
                            M  can cause the transition of strain hardening behavior from linear to nonlinear  [72,73] . Therefore, the increase in  V 
                            M  is responsible for the two-stage strain hardening behavior in IA-750 and IA-800, and increasing strain hardening exponent with rising IA temperature. Notably, the strain hardening exponents in Stage I for IA-750 and IA-800 are lower than those in Stage II, implying a reduced strain hardening rate due to the co-deformation of both the ferrite and martensite phases  [74] .

Additionally, the transition strain between different deformation stages ( ε 
                            tr ) is also a critical factor, as illustrated in  Fig. 12 (f). Observations show that the  ε

                            M . This contradicts the general viewpoint that steels with higher  V

                            tr  
                            [68] . A lower  ε 
                            tr  in F-M DP steels signifies that the martensite undergoes earlier plastic deformation. As  V

                            [74] . This suggests that the Hollomon analysis lacks the precision required to capture the accurate trend. A similar observation was also reported by Mazaheri et al.  [66] .

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
To achieve a simultaneous reduction in the YR and enhancement of tensile strength, a 500 MPa grade HSLA wind power steel manufactured through TMCP was treated by IA at three temperatures followed by water cooling. The microstructure evolution, mechanical properties, and strain hardening behaviors were systematically investigated. The main conclusions are summarized as follows. 
                         
                            1. 
                            After IA treatment, the experimental steel transformed from a predominantly bainitic microstructure to a ferrite-martensite F-M DP structure. The highest  V 
                               M  and a networked martensite distribution were observed in IA-800. The volume fraction and average grain size of the martensite islands, along with the number fraction of HAGBs, exhibited a consistent increase with rising IA temperature. 
                         
                         
                            2. 
                            After IA treatment, the tensile strength increased from 722 MPa to 877 MPa while the yield strength decreased from 622 MPa to 459 MPa. Grain refinement and dislocation-precipitate interactions are the two primary strengthening mechanisms contributing to the yield strength of the IA samples. However, in IA-800 the ferritic matrix was pre-strained by the stress fields of martensite, leading to the decrease in yield strength compared with IA-720 and IA-800. 
                         
                         
                            3. 
                            After IA treatment, the yield ratio was effectively reduced from 0.85 to 0.52. The minimal YR achieved in IA-800 is attributed to the synergistic effect of the high  V 
                               M  and the networked distribution of martensite islands; specifically, the former reduced the  b  value, while the latter suppressed the decline of the  N  value. 
                         
                         
                            4. 
                            Hollomon and MC-J analyses revealed distinct strain hardening characteristics among the different samples. AR and IA-720 exhibited one-stage strain hardening regardless of the model used, while IA-750 and IA-800 displayed two-stage and three-stage regimes, respectively. The strain hardening exponent increased with  V 
                               M . In comparison with the Hollomon model, the MC-J model provides a more accurate representation of the transition strain in F-M DP steels.
